The transcript

0:00 / 0:00

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

James had offered Emma five minutes, not his trust. They were already in the kitchen. James introduced his mother, Nora, and stayed nearby. She was by the window, looking past the wet glass towards a garden that needed attention. Emma let the silence continue. She had learned that people sometimes needed room to decide what they were prepared to say.

“When Claire disappeared, everyone wanted a clear story,” Nora said at last. “An argument, an accident, a stranger in the night. Something with a beginning and an end.”

“What did you tell them?”

“That I had seen her on the evening she went missing. It was true. But it wasn't the whole truth.”

Emma took out her notebook without opening it. “What was missing?”

Nora pulled out a chair and sat down. “I was coming home along the road. It wasn't late, but the light was beginning to go. There was a car stopped near the turning. Claire was standing beside it with a bag.”

“Are you sure it was Claire?”

“Yes. I'd known her for years. I recognised her before I was close enough to speak.”

“Did you speak to her?”

“No. I hesitated. By the time I had decided whether to call out, she'd opened the passenger door and climbed inside. Then the car left.”

Emma waited before asking the question that mattered most. “Did anyone make her get in?”

“Not that I saw.” Nora frowned. “Please don't turn that into something it isn't.”

“What do you mean?”

“For years I've thought: if she opened the door herself, perhaps she wanted to go. But wanting to leave and feeling that you have no other choice can look exactly the same from the other side of a road.”

Emma finally opened her notebook.

“Could you see her face?”

“Not well enough to tell you whether she was frightened. And I didn't see what happened before I arrived.”

“Did you tell the police about the car?”

“I told them I had seen Claire that evening. I remember being asked several questions. But I don't know whether I described every detail, and I won't pretend I remember the exact words now.”

Emma made a note of that distinction. A witness's memory of an event was one thing; a witness's memory of a conversation about the event, fifteen years later, was another.

“Why speak about it now?” she asked.

“Because I keep hearing people speak about Claire as though they already know what happened. I stayed quiet because I wasn't certain. But my silence didn't make anyone more certain, did it?”

“No,” Emma said. “It didn't.”

Nora looked directly at her. “If you use this, don't make her sound carefree. Don't say she went willingly just because you didn't see someone force her.”

“I won't,” Emma replied. “I'll distinguish what you witnessed from what neither of us can know.”

Outside, the light was fading. Emma had found a new account of Claire's last evening, but it left the most difficult question untouched: whether the choice she appeared to make had been a free one.
